processing: A cultivar rather than a finished tea, suited to black tea, green tea and pu-erh. As sheng, the leaf is withered, fixed, rolled, sun-dried and usually pressed, as with other Yunnan raw pu-erh.
harvest_season: Spring picking is the most valued, as with Yunnan teas generally; the cultivar itself buds mid-season.
appearance_dry: Large, long leaves, as is typical of Yunnan large-leaf cultivars.
appearance_liquor: Pale golden yellow in young sheng, as is usual for raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Long elliptic large leaves, olive green in young sheng.
taste_profile: Tasting notes specific to the cultivar are poorly documented. Expect the strength and bitterness typical of young large-leaf Yunnan tea, with results depending much on the processing.

brewing.notes: Treat young sheng from this cultivar like other large-leaf Yunnan raw tea: water a little under boiling and very short first steeps to hold back bitterness.

vintage_note: Rarely named on a label, since cultivar tea usually goes into blends or into cakes and black teas sold by their factory name. As sheng it is sold by harvest year like other raw pu-erh, and as black or green tea it is usually sold as the current year's crop.
description:
Yunkang 14 is a tea plant variety more than a tea you order by name. It is a clonal, tree-type, large-leaf cultivar bred by the Tea Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, and China recognises it as a national variety.

It was selected from the plant population of Nannuo Mountain in Menghai and grows tall, with long elliptic leaves angled a little upward. Its value is practical: it resists cold, drought, disease and pests well, and it can make black tea, green tea or pu-erh.

Its cup depends heavily on what was made from it, and little has been written about its own character. As young sheng, expect what Yunnan large-leaf material typically gives, plenty of strength and some bitterness, so keep the first steeps very short.

You will rarely see it on the label. It is grown widely across Xishuangbanna, Pu'er, Lincang and Baoshan, so it may be in your tea without your knowing. If a seller names it, that tells you the tea comes from planted cultivar bushes, not old trees, so a price that claims old-tree material should make you ask questions.
history:
The institute bred the variety between 1973 and 1985, using single-plant selection from the Nannuo Mountain population in Menghai County. National recognition came in 1987 from the national crop variety approval committee, under the number GS13051-1987.

Besides its large plantings across southern and western Yunnan, it has been introduced to Sichuan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Hunan and Fujian.
